host.name: zbook
host.gpu: AMD Radeon 8060S (gfx1151, Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, 40 CU, unified LPDDR5X)
host.note: Every figure is gfx1151. No gfx1100 hardware was available.

change: Block geometry: WAVES 4 -> 12 (128 -> 384 threads), ROWS_PER_BLOCK 32 -> 96, K_BATCH 64 -> 32. The lane-to-column mapping is unchanged (16 columns per wave, so 8 query rows x 2 query heads), which is what made a larger block possible without touching the fragment code. Shared memory is now 60928 B (shared_query 192x136 + shared_tile 32x136) against 34816 B before, so one block per CU either way; the win is 3 waves per SIMD instead of 2 and shorter per-batch dependency chains.
why: The kernel was at 7.5 TFLOP/s, 15% of the device's fp16 peak, while the reference's own attention kernel reached 12.4 TFLOP/s. A static ISA count showed 2902 instructions per key batch of which 64 are WMMA, and the wave arithmetic (1312 waves over 40 CUs x 4 SIMD, 11.2M cycles) puts the kernel at ~11 cycles per instruction: latency-bound at 2 waves per SIMD rather than issue- or WMMA-bound. That predicted a geometry change rather than an instruction-count change, and the first three instruction-level attempts (vectorizing the K fragment, launch_bounds occupancy hints) were measured as no-ops -- the K-fragment change produced a byte-identical ISA, so the compiler had already vectorized it.

kernel_time_at_production_shape.shape: 1299 rows, 1396 AR keys (2695 total), 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads, head_dim 128
kernel_time_at_production_shape.command: python3 scripts/yue2_attention_bench.py --kernel {scalar,wmma} --repeat 15, alternating in one session
kernel_time_at_production_shape.rocprof_smoke: rocprofv3 --kernel-trace on the same bench: 21 calls, 2.533 ms/call, VGPR 224 (was 248), LDS 60928
kernel_time_at_production_shape.note: The tensor-core kernel is now faster than the reference's own attn_fwd dispatch (2.31 ms) on the same shape.

geometry_sweep.launch_bounds_note: The occupancy hint (min blocks per CU) never helped: with the same geometry, 1, 2, 3 and 4 all measured within noise, because the shared-memory footprint already limits the block count to one per CU.
geometry_sweep.lds_limit: WAVES=12 with K_BATCH=64 exceeds the 65536-byte limit (69632), and WAVES=14 with K_BATCH=8 does too, so WAVES=12/K_BATCH=32 is the corner of the feasible region.
geometry_sweep.paired_ab: K_BATCH=32 and K_BATCH=64 at WAVES=8 are identical within noise (2.59/2.60, 2.70/2.68, 2.82/2.81 over three paired rounds), so K_BATCH was chosen at the value that fits the larger block rather than on a timing difference.

production_profile_gates.unit_tests: 23/23 in tests/test_unit_yue2_nar_kernels.py, including seven WMMA shapes against the independent FP64 NumPy reference and the geometry guard; 48/48 in the NAR runtime, operator and fixture modules (multi-chunk and visibility restriction included)
production_profile_gates.conclusion: All three gates pass. The batch size changed from 64 keys to 32, so the online-softmax batching (and therefore the rounding) changed by design; this stays a production-profile variant with nar_attention_f32 as the registered strict fallback.

end_to_end.determinism: bit-identical across two solves of the same input

twelve_case_replay.passed: 12/12 with exact frame and sample counts

across_the_suite.note: At two steps the attention is a small share of the solve, so the suite-level per-step ratio moves much less than the 32-step product number.

next_candidates: The projections are now the largest item by a wide margin (14.7 s of a 26.07 s solve, 229 ms per evaluation) and run at 16.0 TFLOP/s against 19.4 TFLOP/s for the same shapes launched back to back by hipBLASLt; past ~20 TFLOP/s needs a hand-written GEMM.
The attention is now at the reference's rate, so further work there has to beat it rather than catch it.
